generic: Iron Hydroxide Polymaltose Complex (Iron(III)-hydroxide polymaltose, IPC)
cls: Oral iron preparation - non-ionic iron(III) complex
quick: 100-200 mg elemental iron daily (treatment of iron-deficiency anaemia)
May be taken with or immediately after food - good tolerability, less affected by food than ferrous salts
Acceptable; widely used for iron deficiency in pregnancy (esp. 2nd/3rd trimester)
No specific adjustment; caution and iron monitoring in chronic kidney disease
Caution in iron-overload states/liver disease; no routine dose change
summary: Iron(III)-hydroxide polymaltose complex (IPC) is a non-ionic oral iron preparation in which polynuclear iron(III) hydroxide is stabilised by a polymaltose shell, mimicking physiological ferritin. Iron is released in a controlled, mucosa-regulated manner, giving better gastrointestinal tolerability and fewer interactions than ionic ferrous salts. It is used to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anaemia. All dosing is expressed as elemental iron.
indications: Prophylaxis of iron deficiency (including in pregnancy and lactation)
Latent iron deficiency (low stores without overt anaemia)

dosage.t: Once daily or in divided doses
dosage.n: Continue until Hb normal, then 1-3 months more to replenish stores
Lower dose for prevention without anaemia
Continue at least until delivery to restore stores
Use age-appropriate drops/syrup; follow product labelling

admin: Take with or immediately after meals to optimise tolerability
Tablets/chewable may be chewed or swallowed; drops/syrup can be mixed with fruit/vegetable juice or food
Does not stain teeth as readily as ferrous salts, but rinse after liquid forms
Dosing is by elemental iron content - check product strength
Treatment of anaemia typically continues for 3-5 months and then further to replenish stores
moa: Provides iron as a stable polynuclear iron(III)-hydroxide core surrounded by a polymaltose (polysaccharide) shell, structurally analogous to physiological ferritin. Iron is not freely ionic, so it is absorbed by controlled, competitive ligand exchange across the intestinal mucosa rather than passive diffusion, reducing free-radical generation, gastrointestinal irritation and drug/food chelation. Absorbed iron is incorporated into haemoglobin and replenishes body iron stores.

absolute: Disturbances of iron utilisation (e.g. lead anaemia, sideroachrestic anaemia, thalassaemia without iron deficiency)
Anaemia not due to iron deficiency (unless coexisting deficiency proven)
relative: Chronic kidney disease with risk of iron overload
monitor: Signs of iron overload with prolonged use

preg: Considered acceptable and widely used to treat or prevent iron deficiency in pregnancy; correcting maternal iron deficiency is beneficial. Use according to demonstrated need and local guidance.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding. Iron requirements remain high postpartum and during lactation; small amounts of iron pass into milk and are not considered harmful.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for renal impairment, but oral iron alone is often insufficient in chronic kidney disease/dialysis where parenteral iron may be preferred. Monitor iron indices to avoid overload.
hepatic: No routine dose change; use with caution in liver disease and avoid in iron-overload conditions. Monitor iron stores.

moderate: Oral tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (separate dosing; chelation - less marked than with ferrous salts)
Levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, levodopa, methyldopa, penicillamine (reduced absorption if co-administered; separate by 2-3 hours)
minor: Antacids and proton pump inhibitors (may modestly reduce iron absorption)
interactions.food: Non-ionic iron is comparatively less affected by food, tea, coffee, eggs or dairy than ferrous salts, so it may be taken with meals to improve tolerability
interactions.diagnostics: May cause dark/black stools and can give false-positive guaiac (occult blood) tests; high oral iron can transiently affect serum iron measurements

common: Tooth discolouration with liquid forms (less common than ferrous salts)
serious: Iron accumulation/overload with inappropriate prolonged use
emergency: Acute iron toxicity in accidental overdose, particularly in young children

monitoring: Haemoglobin and reticulocyte count to confirm response
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation before, during and after therapy
Assessment of iron stores to avoid overload with prolonged use
counsel: Iron-deficiency anaemia needs prolonged treatment - continue for several months even after blood counts normalise to refill iron stores
Stools may turn dark or black - this is harmless
Can be taken with or after food, which improves tolerability
Keep all iron products out of reach of children - overdose can be life-threatening in toddlers
Tell your clinician about thyroid medication, antibiotics or other tablets so dosing can be separated
pk: Haematological (reticulocyte) response usually within about 1 week; symptom/Hb improvement over weeks
Controlled, mucosa-regulated absorption without a sharp serum iron peak (contrasts with ferrous salts)
Not a standard concept; absorbed iron enters the body iron pool and is conserved/recycled
Once-daily dosing usually adequate; full course typically 3-5 months or longer
Store below 25-30 C, protect from moisture; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Not US-FDA-approved as a drug product; marketed in EU/UK/India/Australia (e.g. Maltofer, Ferrum Lek) - data drawn from EMA/SmPC, BNF and manufacturer monographs
All dosing is expressed as ELEMENTAL iron - verify the iron content of each formulation
Better gastrointestinal tolerability and adherence than ferrous sulphate at comparable elemental-iron doses, with similar haemoglobin response
Non-ionic structure means fewer food/drug chelation interactions, so it can be taken with meals
Does not exploit divalent-iron transport, so absorption is slower and steadier
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the usual schedule - do not double up. Consistent daily intake matters more than exact timing for a replacement course.
overdose: Oral iron overdose is a medical emergency, especially in children. Features may include vomiting, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity and shock. The polymaltose complex is comparatively less prone to acute toxicity than ferrous salts because iron is not freely ionic, but large ingestions still require urgent assessment. Contact a poison centre; management is supportive with consideration of chelation (deferoxamine) for significant toxicity.
